summary: Early 2026 shows an unusually deadly pace, with around 606 Mediterranean deaths/missing by late February, marking the deadliest start to a year on record in the IOM dataset.
If March maintains this pace, reaching or exceeding 900 deaths by end-March is plausible; the trajectory into March–April supports a high likelihood of crossing the threshold before April.
Key uncertainties remain (SAR capacity, possible NGO tallies being higher than IOM) but overall factors tilt toward a high probability of ≥900 deaths before the end of April 2026.

justification.synthesis_rationale: All factors point to an upward revision from the base anchor; despite some uncertainty about exact counts and potential undercounting, the convergence of a high early-2026 pace, continued crossings, and constrained SAR capacity leads to a calibrated high probability that the 900-death threshold will be reached before April 2026. Calibration recognizes correlation among factors (e.g., pace and seasonal dynamics) and assigns a near-maximum posterior within the 0.90–0.99 range.

question: Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project record at least 900 Mediterranean migrant deaths in 2026 before April 2026?
summary: Objections identify credible downside risks that could slow the March–April trajectory (e.g., SAR improvements and safer routes) and temper the optimistic pace.
February data (~606 deaths) make hitting 900 by end-March plausible but not guaranteed, so the outcome remains conditional on March dynamics.
Data quality uncertainties could undercount fatalities, while NGO counts sometimes exceed official tallies, introducing upside risk that argues against an overly steep downward adjustment.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections reveal credible downside pressures (pace may slow) and data uncertainties that merit tempering an otherwise high ensemble probability.
justification.adjustment: Deviated downward from the ensemble aggregate to 0.78, justified by plausible March slowdown risks and persistent data quality concerns, while acknowledging upside risk from undercounting and ongoing high departures.

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and safe-route policies
causal-factors.rationale: Expanded SAR operations and calls for safer, regular migration pathways could reduce fatalities, exerting downward pressure on the rising toll. Source: Le Monde (turn0news14).

causal-factors.name: Weather hazards and North Africa departure dynamics
causal-factors.rationale: Harsh seas and winter storms, along with continued departures from Libya/Tunisia, raise the risk of further shipwrecks and fatalities in coming weeks. Sources: Le Monde (turn0news14), Guardian (turn0search0).

causal-factors.name: Data completeness and undercount risk
causal-factors.rationale: IOM notes that many shipwrecks remain unrecorded, and current totals may undercount fatalities, which would push the true tally higher than indicated. Source: Le Monde (turn0news14).

causal-factors.name: Pace of Mediterranean deaths early 2026
causal-factors.rationale: IOM Missing Migrants Project reported about 606 deaths/missing through Feb 24, 2026, implying that if March continues at a high rate, the 900-death threshold by end of March is plausible; this is supported by AP News and The Guardian reporting the same figure by late February.

causal-factors.name: Potential undercount or higher tolls per NGO estimates
causal-factors.rationale: NGO estimates (e.g., Mediterranea Saving Humans, Caminando Fronteras) sometimes exceed IOM figures, suggesting the true toll could be higher than 606 by February, increasing the chance of hitting 900 total earlier than some consensus.

causal-factors.name: Policy/SAR constraints affecting rescues
causal-factors.rationale: Media coverage and policy developments point to ongoing restrictions or strains on search-and-rescue capacity in the Central Mediterranean; reduced rescues can raise fatalities, pushing cumulative deaths higher.

causal-factors.name: March–April seasonal dynamics and potential surge in crossings
causal-factors.rationale: Seasonal patterns often see riskier crossing conditions and higher attempt rates in spring; combined with the strong February pace, there is a non-negligible upside risk to reaching 900 deaths by March.

causal-factors.name: Current pace of Mediterranean deaths/missing through February 2026
causal-factors.rationale: As of February 23–24, 2026, about 606 deaths or missing persons have been recorded on the Central Mediterranean, implying March could add hundreds more if the pace persists.

causal-factors.name: Weather-driven mass shipwrecks and severe storms in early 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Cyclone Harry and related severe weather in January produced additional tragic crossings, signaling high risk conditions that could sustain high fatalities into March.

causal-factors.name: Ongoing high departures from Libya/Tunisia (Central Mediterranean flux)
causal-factors.rationale: Reports indicate continued departures from Tobruk and Tunisian ports, maintaining a large at-sea population exposed to dangerous crossings.

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and policy responses
causal-factors.rationale: IOM and outlets have highlighted calls to strengthen SAR and improve safe pathways; greater rescue capacity could reduce fatalities and slow the pace toward 900 before April.

synthesis: The February pace implies a nonzero chance of reaching 900 by the end of March, but downsides from SAR improvements and data uncertainties warrant a calibrated adjustment below the strongest ensemble signal. A probability around 0.78 with a 0.68–0.86 range reflects these competing forces.
